title: An Energy-Efficient Kalman Filter Architecture with Tunable Accuracy for Brain-Computer Interfaces
problem: Kalman Filters are standard for BCIs to predict motion from brain activity, but hardware implementations specialized for embedded BCI constraints (latency-accuracy tuning, energy efficiency) are lacking.
motivation: BCI applications require specialized hardware acceleration of signal processing with fine-grained control over latency and accuracy tradeoffs to enable real-time neural decoding on power-limited embedded systems.
method: The researchers built a hardware accelerator — a specialized circuit that runs Kalman Filters, which predict motion from brain signals. The hardware is configurable, meaning you can adjust how fast it responds (latency) versus how accurate its predictions are (accuracy). This flexibility lets engineers explore different settings to find the right balance for their specific brain-computer interface. The accelerator plugs into a processor system and can dynamically adjust its settings while processing neural data.
key_novelty: A Kalman Filter hardware accelerator for brain-computer interfaces with precise, adjustable speed-versus-accuracy settings.
contributions: First configurable KF hardware architecture specialized for BCI requirements
Support for fine-grained latency and accuracy tuning enabling design-space exploration
Integration into heterogeneous SoC for practical BCI deployment
15.3x energy-efficiency improvement and 1000x better accuracy compared to state-of-the-art
limitations: Not discussed; evaluation on FPGA prototypes without silicon results.
primary_theme: Configurable Kalman Filter hardware accelerator for brain-computer interfaces
